profiles.name: Research Methods & Statistics
profiles.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
profiles.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
profiles.topics: research design; operationalization; sampling; experiments; surveys; descriptive and inferential statistics
profiles.methods: Research design; Operationalization; Experimental design; Survey research; Sampling; Descriptive statistics; Inferential statistics; ANOVA

profiles.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
profiles.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
profiles.profile: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.
profiles.topics: hough transform for detection of lines; detection of corners; self driving vehicles; feature detection; image; processing

profiles.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
profiles.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
profiles.profile: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).

profiles.name: Introduction to Programming
profiles.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
profiles.profile: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.

profiles.name: Linear Algebra
profiles.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
profiles.profile: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.

profiles.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
profiles.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
profiles.profile: Many problems in science and engineering presented in a mathematical format do not have exact analyt- ical solutions; these problems can only be solved numerically. The nature of the mathematical problem dictates the type of numerical algorithm to use; solving an optimization problem requires a different al- gorithm than solving a differential equation. The prerequisite gateway courseMathematical Methods introduces techniques and methods for solving equations in one variable, for finding derivatives of func- tions, or for solving integrals,etc., analytically. This course focuses on the same mathematical concepts but from a numerical and computational perspective. Numerical solutions obtained through some al- gorithm pose the following challenge: what does the output mean? How sensitive is the algorithm to a wrong input? There are examples showing that numerical algorithms can produce completely wrong and unexpected outputs resulting in a disaster. Numerical and computational mathematics is a broad topic; numerous algorithms exist for numerically solving the same mathematical problem. This courses focuses on algorithms for solving equations in one variable. Several algorithms exist for interpolating or extrapolating functions on the basis of a set of sample points of that function. Numerical methods for differentiation, but especially integration form a set of very important numerical algorithms. The course discusses numerous algorithms for solving ordinary differential equations.

profiles.name: Linear Systems
profiles.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
profiles.profile: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.

profiles.name: Ethics
profiles.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
profiles.profile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
profiles.topics: animal rights; future generations; climate change; historical injustice; moral reasoning virtue; reasoning virtue ethics

profiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
profiles.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
profiles.profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.

profiles.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
profiles.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
profiles.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.

profiles.name: Epidemiology & Public Health

Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

profiles.name: Functional Anatomy
profiles.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
profiles.profile: Functional Anatomy examines the structure of the human body in direct relation to function. In this course, anatomical structures and their functions are systematically studied together, at the level of body systems as well as individual anatomical components. The course is organised in thematic blocks, each addressing a specific anatomical region or system (the Skeletal System & Vertebral Column; Bony Thorax & Pelvis; Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems; Abdomen; Reproductive & Lower Urinary Systems) and each emphasising specific anatomical and functional reasoning (rather than exhaustive memorisation). Within these blocks, learning activities are purposefully selected to support the intended learning outcomes, combining visual, spatial and experiential approaches. Anatomical understanding is developed through surface anatomy, medical imaging, scientific anatomical drawing and video-based human remain based material, complemented by carefully framed encounters with human skeletal remains, a dissection facility and in class clinical demonstrations. Together, these activities foster three-dimensional anatomical insight, spatial reasoning and awareness of anatomical variation. Please note that these are explicitly framed as academic learning experiences rather than clinical skills training. Studying human anatomy inevitably confronts students with an ethical paradox: respect for the human body is taught through its objectification for scientific study.

profiles.name: Pharmacology
profiles.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
profiles.profile: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.

profiles.name: Infection & Immunity
profiles.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
profiles.profile: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.

profiles.profile: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. profiles.name: Neurobiology
profiles.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
profiles.profile: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.

profiles.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
profiles.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
profiles.profile: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.

profiles.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
profiles.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
profiles.profile: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. profiles.name: Molecular Cell Biology
profiles.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
profiles.profile: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. profiles.name: Human Physiology
profiles.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
profiles.profile: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.

profiles.name: Biochemistry
profiles.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
profiles.profile: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.

Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.

profiles.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.

profiles.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
profiles.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
profiles.profile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.

profiles.name: Medical & Health Psychology
profiles.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
profiles.profile: In th is course, Medical and Health Psychology , we will examine the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and socio-cultural factors that influence health and illness. Guided by the core principle of the field, the bio-psycho-social approach of the human being, we will explore key theories, research findings, and specific interventions within clinical health psychology, with a particular focus on the role of psychological expertise and mental health professionals in medical settings. profiles.name: Advanced Research Seminar
profiles.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
profiles.profile: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.

profiles.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
profiles.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
profiles.profile: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.

profiles.name: Persuasive Communication
profiles.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
profiles.profile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.

profiles.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”.
